chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa — all from Ibn Mahbub, from Durust ibn Abi Mansur, from Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Hamid, from Abu al-Hasan Musa ibn Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:
A discussion with the scholar upon the rubbish dump is better than a discussion with the ignorant upon the carpets.

key_terms.الزَّرَابِيّ: Richly woven carpets or cushions — symbol of comfort and luxury
key_terms.الْجَاهِل: The ignorant one, the unlearned — contrasted with the scholar
key_terms.الْعَالِم: The learned one, the scholar of religious knowledge
key_terms.الْمَزَابِل: Rubbish heaps, refuse dumps — symbol of lowly, uncomfortable places
key_terms.مُحَادَثَة: Conversing, sitting and speaking with; companionship through dialogue

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Kazim say about the value of sitting with a scholar vs. an ignorant person?
ai.summary: Imam Musa al-Kazim (peace be upon him) draws a vivid contrast between two types of gatherings: sitting with a knowledgeable person even in the most humble and uncomfortable of settings is superior to sitting with an ignorant person in conditions of luxury. This teaching invites the listener to prioritize the company of scholars over material comfort, reflecting the Shia tradition's deep emphasis on religious knowledge as the highest social good. The audience of this hadith — students of hadith in Kufa and Qum — would have understood 'al-mazabil' (rubbish heaps) and 'al-zarabi' (rich carpets/cushions) as a deliberate rhetorical contrast designed to make the lesson memorable.
